message.content:
The mother sea dragon swept across the upper room and settled beside the lighthouse nest. Daylight gleamed on the brass compass between her jaws.

Ekin stopped breathing.

The dragon lowered her head and placed the compass in the nest. Ekin saw it land within reach—or almost within reach. Her grandfather’s compass looked so small beside the dragon.

“There,” Ekin whispered. She stepped forward.

Duru caught her attention with a sharp hiss. “Wait.”

Ekin turned impatiently. Duru was staring past the mother dragon, not at the compass. Following her gaze, Ekin noticed a cat-sized dragon hatchling crouched close to the nest. Its wings shifted, but it did not fly. It appeared uninjured, only watchful.

“A hatchling,” Duru said quietly.

“I can see that.” Ekin’s eyes snapped back to the compass. “And I can see what I came for.”

She edged toward the nest.

The mother sea dragon moved at once. She spread herself across the approach, planting her body between Ekin and the nest. Her head lowered. She did not speak, but the warning in her stance was plain.

Ekin halted. The compass shone behind the dragon.

Duru glanced toward the far side of the upper room. A narrow turning stair descended toward the lower maintenance room. From where they stood, both girls could see down the curve to the fixed sea-facing iron grate below.

Ekin followed Duru’s look, then frowned. “That stair doesn’t get me to the compass.”

“Walking straight at her won’t either,” Duru warned.

“It’s right there.”

“So is she.”

Ekin clenched her hands inside her jacket sleeves. Duru was probably right, which made the warning more annoying, not less. She stayed in the upper room, staring past the blocking dragon at the brass compass in the nest.
